messages.subject: Infinite Deviance
parts:
Hello all,

 

I encountered an issue of infinite deviance. I would appreciate it if anyone could give me an advice what I might be doing wrong.

I wrote a state space model to estimate survival probabilities and detection probabilities using JAGS. Traceplots, Rhats and effective sample sizes look good for all the parameters. However, I get infinite deviance. I tried it both with flat priors and informative priors, and deviance came out infinite with either model.

I wondered if I don’t have enough data for the number of parameters, so I tried with a half of the parameters fixed to see what would happen. The deviance still came back infinity.

 

Thank you,

Meg

messages.subject: Re: Infinite Deviance
parts: Just a shot in the dark, but perhaps you have missing values lurking in either your data or your covariates somewhere that is compromising deviance? Hard to say without actually seeing the code and data. You might need to post a reproducible example. I often find that in the process of boiling my data and code down into a reproducible example, I find the error.

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Infinite Deviance
parts:
Hi Meg,

I agree it would help to say more about your model.  The term state-space model can encompass quite a bit these days.

In a population dynamics state-space model, it is not uncommon for one of the variance components to have a maximum likelihood estimate of 0 (i.e. a precision of infinite).  Examples of where I think this has been discussed (IIRC!) include de Valpine and Hilborn (2005, https://doi.org/10.1139/f05-116, mea culpa for the self-ref), Knape (2008, https://doi.org/10.1890/08-0071.1) , and Auger-Méthe et al. (2016, https://www.nature.com/articles/srep26677).  It doesn't necessarily mean there is something wrong.  A confidence region around the MLE would still include non-zero variance values (i.e. meaningful, finite precision values).  But sometimes in a Bayesian context the choice of priors can really matter in these cases.  Some priors will lose reasonable coverage properties by allowing the posterior to have too much probability mass (possibly improperly) for enormous precision values, for example.

I hope that helps.

Perry
